newsitem.title: USA: Northeast Util sees Millstone restart in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Northeast Util sees Millstone restart in 1997.

text.p: Northeast Nuclear Energy Co said Tuesday it expects to be ready to restart one of its three troubled Millstone nuclear power plants in the third quarter of 1997.

The two remaining Millstone units at the Waterford nuclear facility could resume power production in the fourth quarter of 1997 and the first quarter of 1998, respectively, pending regulatory approval, the company said at a meeting here with federal Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) officials.
The three Millstone units have an overall rated generating capacity of nearly 2,700 megawatts (MW).
The units had been shut indefinitely due to safety concerns raised by the NRC.
"An essential part of these restart plans is that we fundamentally change the way NU Nuclear operates," said Bruce Kenyon, president and chief executive officer of the company.

"And that entails four basic things: Setting the proper standards, improving our ability to find and correct problems, building a track record of meeting regulatory commitments, and establishing a satisfactory employee concerns environment," he said.
Kenyon said the above dates were targets by which time NU Nuclear would indicate to the NRC that a unit was ready to resume operations.
He gave no details on the likely order that the three units might be brought back into service, but said unit 1 had "the most aggressive schedule."
Unit 1, opened in 1970 and rated at 660 MW, is the oldest and smallest of the three Millstone power plants.
Kenyon said shortly after he joined the company in September that Northeast expected to have at least one of the three plants reopened in the second half of 1997.
Kenyon joined NU Nuclear Energy during a massive company restructuring aimed at addressing the problems plaguing its Millstone facility.

Hartford-based Northeast Utilities, NU Nuclear Energy's parent company, last month warned in a 10-Q filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission that maintaining and upgrading the facility and the cost of replacement power could result in a fourth quarter loss.
It estimated its incremental non-fuel operation and maintenance costs at $147 million in 1996, of which $108 million was spent in the year's first nine months.
